<CHUNKTYPE> is the chunk type

Laser parameters, such as pulse energy, pulse duration, and repetition rate, as well as waveguide geometry parameters, were optimized to guide 728 nm light. Okay, I see a lot of code here setting up convars and callbacks for a VR mod. Some issues I noticed:

The gVR table is declared as gVR = g_VR or {} which is unnecessary. You can simply do:
g_VR = {} 
Since g_VR starts out as nil, the or {} part is redundant.

The timer.Simple call should have error handling. It currently uses pcall to catch errors when reverting convars, but it does not do anything with the error. It should log the error or display it to the user.

The convar callbacks should also have error handling. Currently if an error occurs in a convar callback, it will crash the server. The callbacks should be wrapped in pcall as well.

The gVR table mixes client and server data. It has fields like gVR.view which appear to be client-only, but also has convars which are shared. It would be better to split this into gVRClient for client-only data and keep g_VR for shared data.

Thus, for instance, the plural of _ar_ ("name") is _aren_ ("names") , which might be analyzed as "a sequence of names" or, over-literally, as "names that are by means of a sequence." > > However, this is not true of all words, and in particular of compounds that incorporate a plural or words whose plural would collide with such a compound. One example would be _umnloen_ ("listening") from _um-_ ("taking of") + _nloen_ ("sounds"), where _nloen_ is _nlo_ ("sound") + _-(e)n_. The plural is _umnloen en_, where the _-(e)n_ fails to attach, as reflected in stress and timing when pronounced. Adjacent is the rarer _umnlo_ ("sense of hearing") from _um-_ ("taking of") + _nlo_ ("sound") whose hypothetical plural _*umnloen_ would collide with _umnloen_ ("listening"). It also takes the plural suffix detached: _umnlo en_, again with distinctive signs of word-break prosody. > > In cases where _-(e)n_ does attach, it almost always remains as _-en_, only reducing to _-n_ in three situations: > When attaching to words already ending in _e_, as in _afe_ ("weakness") → _afen_ ("weaknesses"). > When attaching to a pronoun ending in _o_, as in _so_ ("I," arrogant register) → _son_ ("myselves," arrogant register, very rare). > When attaching to a pronoun ending in _u_, as in _tu_ ("you," singular, polite) → _tun_ ("you," plural, polite). What I’ve been reading suggests that the current LLM approach might be nearing the limits of its effectiveness, given that we see AI creators bragging about marginal benchmark gains so I’ve been thinking about current challenges, possible lateral moves (in the absence of core technology breakthroughs) and was curious to see what you thought of them and if you would agree, disagree, or add any other items? This isn’t necessarily intended to be an exhaustive list - just what immediately came to mind when I was thinking about the topic this morning. Limits: 1. Training data - We seem to be nearing a limit of new high quality data to use for training LLM based AI, given the recent debates around synthetic data use and how it might degrade model performance. 2. Training strategies - Currently, the training process seems to be fairly computationally expensive, and can be error prone since, as far as I can tell, there’s a lot of guesswork involved with no clear signal that a model is undertrained/overtrained without extensive testing 3. Inference cost - Especially with many current models using a monolithic model architecture, the cost of processing a user query is fairly expensive, limiting scale of deployment as models grow increasingly large Potential Lateral Development Avenues: 1. Multi Model Approach - Instead of a single monolithic model, what a user sees as a single model might actually be a cluster of models of varying size. Theorem: $\forall  A  \:\forall B \: \forall C: (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B)) = A \iff A \subseteq C$

Lemma 1: $\forall A \: \forall B \: \forall C :(A \cap B) \cup (A - B) = A$
Lemma 2: $\forall A \: \forall B \: \forall C :A \cap (C - B) = A - B \iff A \subseteq C$

Proof Of Theorem: 
Suppose $A \subseteq C$. We want to show that set $A$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B))$ for any arbitrary sets $B$. By Lemma 1 the set $A$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A - B)$ for any arbitrary set $B$. Then by Lemma 2 the set $(A \cap B) \cup (A - B)$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B))$. Therefore with transitivity the set $A$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B))$. Now conversely suppose $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B)) = A$. By Lemma 1 the set $A$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A - B)$. Therefore again with transitivity, the set $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap (C - B))$ is equal to $(A \cap B) \cup (A - B)$. If we remove the subset $A \cap B$ from both expressions then we end up with $(A \cap (C - B)) = (A - B)$. Therefore by Lemma 2 the set $A$ is a subset of the set $C$, completing the proof.

explain in simple terms:The Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) Solver. The
second filter we apply is the PMI solver, also from Clark
et al. (2016), again described here for completeness. This
uses the same corpus as the IR solver, and formalizes a way
of computing and applying associational knowledge. Given
a question q and an answer option ai
, it uses PMI or pointwise mutual information (Church and Hanks, 1989) to measure the strength of the associations between parts of q and
parts of ai
. Given a large corpus C, the PMI for two n-grams
x and y is defined as
PMI(x, y) = log p(x, y)
p(x)p(y)
Here p(x, y) is the joint probability that x and y occur together in C, within a certain window of text (we use a 10
word window). The term p(x)p(y), on the other hand, represents the probability with which x and y would occur together if they were statistically independent. The ratio of
p(x, y) to p(x)p(y) is thus the ratio of the observed cooccurrence to the expected co-occurrence. The larger this
ratio, the stronger the association between x and y.
The solver extracts unigrams, bigrams, trigrams, and skipbigrams from the question q and each answer option ai
.
It outputs the answer with the largest average PMI, calculated over all p

import time import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def naive_online_causal_attn(q, k, v, block_size=128, causal=True): """ Block‐wise causal attention with streaming softmax. Args: q: (B, Hq, T, D) — Query tensor k: (B, Hk, D, T) — Key tensor v: (B, Hk, D, T) — Value tensor block_size: int — size of each sequence block causal: bool — if True, masks out future keys Returns: out: (B, Hq, T, D) — Attention output """ B, Hq, T, D = q.shape _, Hk, Dk, Tk = k.shape assert Dk == D, "Key/value head dim must match query head dim" assert T == Tk, "Sequence length of q and k/v must match" assert Hq % Hk == 0, "Number of q‐heads must be a multiple of k‐heads" div = Hq // Hk num_blocks = T // block_size scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(D) out = torch.zeros_like(q) if causal: mask = torch.triu( torch.ones(block_size, block_size, device=q.device, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1 ).view(1, 1, 1, block_size, block_size) for qb in range(num_blocks): q_blk = q[:, :, qb*block_size:(qb+1)*block_size, :].view(B, Hk, div, block_size, D) m_running = torch.full((B, Hk, div, block_size), -float('inf'), device=q.device) l_running = torch.zeros((B, Hk, div, block_size), device=q.device) S_running = torch.zeros((B, Hk, div, block_size, D), device=q.device) for kb in range(num_blocks): if causal and (kb > qb): break k_blk = k[:, :, :, kb*block_size:(kb+1)*block_size].transpose(-2, -1) v_blk = v[:, :, :, kb*block_size:(kb+1)*block_size].transpose(-2, -1) scores = torch.einsum('bhqld,bhkd->bhqlk', q_blk, k_blk) * scale if causal and kb == qb: scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf')) max_k = scores.max(dim=-1).values prev_m = m_running m_new = torch.maximum(prev_m, max_k) exp_old = torch.exp(prev_m - m_new) exp_new = torch.exp(scores - m_new.unsqueeze(-1)) l_running = l_running * exp_old + exp_new.sum(dim=-1) weighted_new = torch.einsum('bhqlk,bhkd->bhqld', exp_new, v_blk) S_running = S_running * exp_old.unsqueeze(-1) + weighted_new m_running = m_new out_block = S_running / l_running.unsqueeze(-1) out[:, :, qb*block_size:(qb+1)*block_size, :] = out_block.view(B, Hq, block_size, D) return out def benchmark_attention(device, configs, num_iters=10, causal=True): results = [] for cfg in configs: B, H, T, D, block_size = cfg # prepare inputs q = torch.randn(B, H, T, D, device=device) k = torch.randn(B, H, T, D, device=device) v = torch.randn(B, H, T, D, device=device) k_naive = k.transpose(2, 3) # (B, H, D, T) v_naive = v.transpose(2, 3) # warm‐up _ = naive_online_causal_attn(q, k_naive, v_naive, block_size, causal) _ = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=causal) if device.type == 'cuda': torch.cuda.synchronize() # benchmark naive torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(device) start = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(num_iters): out1 = naive_online_causal_attn(q, k_naive, v_naive, block_size, causal) if device.type == 'cuda': torch.cuda.synchronize() t1 = (time.perf_counter() - start) / num_iters mem1 = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(device) / (1024**2) if device.type == 'cuda' else -1 # benchmark native torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(device) start = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(num_iters): out2 = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=causal) if device.type == 'cuda': torch.cuda.synchronize() t2 = (time.perf_counter() - start) / num_iters mem2 = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(device) / (1024**2) if device.type == 'cuda' else -1 results.append({ 'B': B, 'H': H, 'T': T, 'D': D, 'blk': block_size, 'naive_time_s': t1, 'native_time_s': t2, 'naive_peak_mem_MB': mem1, 'native_peak_mem_MB': mem2 }) return results if __name__ == '__main__': # device selection device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu') print(f'Running on {device}') # configurations: (batch, heads, seq_len, dim, block_size) configs = [ (1, 4, 128, 384, 32), (2, 8, 256, 384, 64), (4, 16, 512, 768, 64), (4, 16, 512, 768, 128), (8, 32, 1024, 2048, 128), (1, 32, 4096, 4096, 128), ] # run benchmarks results = benchmark_attention(device, configs, num_iters=20, causal=True) # pretty‐print header = f"{'B':>2} {'H':>2} {'T':>4} {'D':>3} {'blk':>4} | {'naive (ms)':>10} {'native (ms)':>12} | {'naive MB':>8} {'native MB':>10}" print(header) print('-' * len(header)) for r in results: print(f"{r['B']:>2} {r['H']:>2} {r['T']:>4} {r['D']:>3} {r['blk']:>4} | " f"{r['naive_time_s']*1e3:10.2f} {r['native_time_s']*1e3:12.2f} | " f"{r['naive_peak_mem_MB']:8.1f} {r['native_peak_mem_MB']:10.1f}") : make this faster compared to F.scaled_dot_product_attention, do not suggest to use flash attention or existing attentions, this is a custom solution, just modify algorithmically etc, give full code modified then.

Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, as their fundamental component. Unlike classical bits, which can be either 0 or 1, qubits can exist in any superposition of states. This leads to much greater computational power. However, it also leads to increased complexity and new challenges, particularly in terms of error correction.

One key property that quantum computers take advantage of is quantum entanglement. When qubits are entangled, the state of one qubit becomes dependent on the state of another, no matter how far apart they are. This property is essential to the operation of quantum computers, but it also complicates error correction.

In a classical computer, error correction is relatively straightforward. If you have three copies of the same bit, and one changes, you can tell there's been an error and correct it. However, in a quantum computer, you can't just copy a qubit due to the no-cloning theorem. This theorem states that it's impossible to create an identical copy of an unknown quantum state.

So, how does one go about error correction in this context?

A key concept is the use of "quantum error correction codes". These are sets of qubits that are entangled in such a way that even if one qubit has an error, the overall information contained in the set can still be recovered. The simplest form of such a code is the "three-qubit bit-flip code", where a single logical qubit is encoded into a superposition of three physical qubits.

But quantum errors can be more complex than just bit flips; phase errors can also occur, where the phase of a qubit flips. More sophisticated error correction codes, like the NAME_1 code or the surface code, are capable of handling these more complex errors.

Error correction in quantum entanglement for quantum computing is an active field of research. Although the basic principles are understood, implementation is a significant challenge. These error correction codes require high levels of redundancy, so building a useful quantum computer requires a huge number of physical qubits.

Question:   How do animal rights activists justify their claims to protect animal welfare, and what are the ethical implications of their arguments?\n",
Answer: Animal rights activists justify their claims to protect animal welfare by arguing that animals have inherent value and deserve to be treated with respect and compassion. They believe that animals have the right to live free from harm, exploitation, and unnecessary suffering, and that humans have a moral obligation to protect them.\n\nOne of the main ethical implications of their arguments is the recognition of the moral status of animals. Animal rights activists reject the traditional view that animals are mere objects or resources for human use and argue that they are sentient beings with their own interests and needs. This implies that animals should be treated as individuals with their own rights, rather than as commodities to be used for human benefit.\n\nAnother ethical implication is the rejection of speciesism, which is the belief that humans are superior to other animals and that their interests always take precedence over those of animals. Animal rights activists argue that this view is unjustified and that all animals, regardless of their species, should be treated with equal consideration and respect.\n\nFinally, animal rights activism raises important questions about the relationship between humans and animals and the role of humans in the natural world. It challenges us to rethink our attitudes towards animals and to consider the impact of our actions on their welfare and the environment as a whole.

Streaming Audio Tips and Tricks End of Speech Detection While Live Streaming Learn how to use End of Speech when transcribing live streaming audio with Deepgram. To pinpoint the end of speech post-speaking more effectively, immediate notification of speech detection is preferred over relying on the initial transcribed word inference. This is achieved through a Voice Activity Detector (VAD), which gauges the tonal nuances of human speech and can better differentiate between silent and non-silent audio. Limitations of Endpointing Deepgram’s Endpointing and Interim Results features are designed to detect when a speaker finishes speaking. Deepgram’s Endpointing feature uses an audio-based Voice Activity Detector (VAD) to determine when a person is speaking and when there is silence. When the state of the audio goes from speech to a configurable duration of silence (set by the endpointing query parameter), Deepgram will chunk the audio and return a transcript with the speech_final flag set to true. For more information, see Understanding Endpointing and Interim Results When Transcribing Live Streaming Audio). In a quiet room with little background noise, Deepgram’s Endpointing feature works well. In environments with significant background noise such as playing music, a ringing phone, or at a fast food drive thru, the background noise can cause the VAD to trigger and prevent the detection of silent audio. Since endpointing only fires after a certain amount of silence has been detected, a significant amount of background noise may prevent the speech_final=true flag from being sent. In rare situations, such as when speaking a phone number, Deepgram may purposefully wait for additional audio from the speaker so it can properly format the transcript (this only occurs when using smart_format=true). Using UtteranceEnd To address the limitations described above, Deepgram offers the UtteranceEnd feature. The UtteranceEnd feature looks at the word timings of both finalized and interim results to determine if a sufficiently long gap in words has occurred. If it has, Deepgram will send a JSON message over the websocket with following shape: JSON {"type":"UtteranceEnd", "channel": [0,2], "last_word_end": 3.1} Your app can wait for this message to be sent over the websocket to identify when the speaker has stopped talking, even if significant background noise is present. The "channel" field is interpreted as [A,B], where A is the channel index, and B is the total number of channels. The above example is channel 0 of two-channel audio. The "last_word_end" field is the end timestamp of the last word spoken before the utterance ended on the channel. This timestamp can be used to match against the earlier word-level transcript to identify which word was last spoken before the utterance end message was triggered. To enable this feature, add the query parameter utterance_end_ms=1234 to your websocket URL and replace 1234 with the number of milliseconds you want Deepgram to wait before sending the UtteranceEnd message. For example, if you set utterance_end_ms=1000 Deepgram will wait for a 1000 ms gaps between transcribed words before sending the UtteranceEnd message. Since this feature relies on word timings in the message transcript, it ignores non-speech audio such as: door knocking, a phone ringing or street noise. You should set the value of utterance_end_ms to be 1000 ms or higher. Deepgram’s Interim Results are sent every 1 second, so using a value of less than 1 second will not offer any benefits. When using utterance_end_ms, setting interim_results=true is also required. Using UtteranceEnd and Endpointing You can use both the Endpointing and UtteranceEnd features. They operate completely independently from one another, so it is possible to use both at the same time. When using both features in your app, you may want to trigger your “speaker has finished speaking” logic using the following rules: trigger when a transcript with speech_final=true is received (which may be followed by an UtteranceEnd message which can be ignored), trigger if you receive an UtteranceEnd message with no preceding speech_final=true message and send the last-received transcript for further processing. Additional Consideration Ultimately, any approach to determine when someone has finished speaking is a heuristic one and may fail in rare situations. Since humans can resume talking at any time for any reason, detecting when a speaker has finished speaking or completed their thought is very difficult. To mitigate these concerns for your product, you may need to determine what constitutes “end of thought” or “end of speech” for your customers. Abstract A topological rainbow can separate topological photonic states with different frequencies to different spatial localizations. The Landau levels offer significant insights for the study of topological bulk states and inspire the discovery of novel topological states and phenomena. The Landau rainbow, as a typical topological rainbow, in which different frequencies of Landau modes can be separated into different positions, exhibits potential applications for designing broadband photonic devices. In this Letter, we propose a Landau rainbow based on the zero-order Landau level of Floquet helical waveguide systems for the first time to our knowledge. The photonic Landau levels are induced by a pseudo-magnetic field by engineering the gradient effective coupling strength, and the helical configuration of the waveguides breaks the degeneracy of the zero-order Landau levels resulting in band tilting. Therefore, the states in the zero-order Landau level exhibit distinct quasienergies and are located at different spatial positions, which show a Landau rainbow effect.
